articles.text: Ted Scherman made a momentary return out of retirement this week to run the 6th Grade Bootcamp at Piedmont Middle School with P.E. teacher Tim Wisnewski. Forty-nine elementary school graduates are taking part in the camp August 3-5, which helps orient the youngest students to their new school. The popular camp was founded by Scherman. “I actually arranged this with the Rec. Dep’t before retiring. It’s just fun, these kids are so excited to be middle schoolers. It’s good to remind me why I taught for so many years too, and then on Thursday, when teachers are prepping their classrooms, I’ll be back in the forest,” said Scherman, who recently returned from a 16-day trek exploring 225 miles of the Pacific rest Trail. Logistically the camp helps incoming 6th graders feel comfortable on the new campus, they get to meet the office staff and take part in scavenger hunts to explore. “There’s no academic lesson you can give in two days, the biggest part of this camp is the social benefit, as kids work together, and eat together. It’s really nice to have some the 8th graders here helping out, that way incoming 6th graders will know a few of the older students on campus,” said Scherman. articles.text: There has been a lot of noise about how homeowners should market their homes for sale. But the most important question is not whether every property should follow the same process. It’s which strategy will best position the seller and their home to achieve the right result. At Compass, we believe sellers should have a choice. They can place their home on the MLS immediately, or they can begin with a phased marketing strategy that allows them to test pricing, gather feedback, and prepare the property before it is presented to the The moment a home is listed on the internet via the MLS or another portal, the clock starts ticking and days on market begin accumulating. This is a statistic that everyone can now see. The asking price becomes an anchor from which buyers negotiate down. When a buyer sees the days on market increase, they perceive there is something wrong with the property. Moreover, public price cuts make the seller appear desperate, which further hurts the seller. Pre-marketing a home gives a seller the opportunity to ready their property, evaluate pricing, gather market feedback, and make informed decisions before their home makes its public debut on the MLS. New research found that homes that use pre-marketing, such as Private Exclusive or Coming Soon, before being listed on the MLS, sell for 4.6% more than homes that go directly to the MLS. They also sell faster and are significantly less likely to experience public price reductions. On a $1.5 million home, a 4.6% premium represents approximately $69,000. For a seller, that difference could become part of a down payment on their next home or provide additional retirement savings and greater financial security. The research findings make sense because a home that enters the public market with the right price, the right presentation, and stronger information on buyer demand is better positioned to succeed. Just as companies in other industries test products before a major launch, sellers should have the ability to gather information and refine their strategy before putting one of their most important financial assets on the market. No single approach will be right for every homeowner. Some sellers will want immediate and maximum public exposure. Others may value privacy, flexibility, or the ability to test the market before their public debut. Both choices should remain available. Real estate professionals, as trusted advisors, have a fiduciary duty to share with a seller the myriad opportunities available before listing directly on the MLS. The seller is not obliged to adhere to the rules of the listing aggregators or third-party websites that don’t have their best interests in mind. That may be one way, but it’s not the only way. At Compass, we offer clients a choice when selling their home, helping them confidently and successfully reach their goals, based on their individual needs. YOU, the homeowner, should decide the best approach to selling your home. Submitted by Kevin Patsel, Regional Vice President, NorCal, Compass

articles.text: Part two Last week I began what I hope will be a series of essays under the umbrella title The Only Constant is Change wherein I referred to the Gutenberg revolution which eventually led to the democratization of reading, an expanding access to books, and the extraordinary impact writing and reading had on countless Shortly after that first Post article appeared, I received by email a remarkable 28-page essay from a fellow Returned Peace Corps Volunteer. He had devoted several decades since returning encouraging those Peace Corps writers who sought to capture in prose the essence and meaning of those two years of service in some of the most challenging and The author of the essay, The End of Reading is Here, was The Atlantic Magazine journalist Rose Horowitch and can be found in the August, 2026 edition. And just under the title is the following caveat: “Optimists once believed that universal literacy was inevitable. Now it seems that the age of reading might be a short anomaly in human history.” When I received the essay I read and reread what was not a prediction of future outcomes, but an affirmative, well documented essay that we have indeed arrived at a second Gutenberg moment. Initially I approached Horowitch’s thesis with skepticism. My earliest memories are of yearning to read, and I soon began collecting comic books filled with graphic stories of superheroes. I was a devoted member of the Dell/Marvel Universe. As were my friends. Before long I had a library card and relished spending afternoons, when not playing ball at the local rec department field, at a small local library. And yet, there was that subtitle qualifier. That word “anomaly.” Horowitch points out that while Americans were once members of a proudly literate society, according to a National Endowment for the Arts comprehensive survey of the nation’s reading habits, “fewer than half of all adults reported having read a book of any kind in 2002. Only 38 percent read a novel or short story.” Horowitch goes on to say: According to an analysis of 236,000 responses to the American Time Use Survey it was found that “the proportion of Americans who read for pleasure on any given day fell from 28 percent in 2004 to 16 percent in 2023. (The study looked at people who had read a book, magazine, or newspaper; listened to an audiobook; or read an e-book.) Gambling has become a more common leisure activity than reading a book. Last year 57 percent of Americans placed a bet.” What has changed, and why? Part three to follow. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: At the council meeting on July 20, councilmembers accepted the 2025 Annual Progress Report for the implementation of the Piedmont General Plan 6th Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element programs. Interim Planning and Building Director Jeff Bond presented the report detailing the City’s ongoing progress toward meeting its State-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation. Last year was determined to be satisfactory, but the council was slightly concerned with the small decline in planning and building permits compared to the past four years. In 2025, the City completed construction of 14 new homes, all of which were accessory dwelling units (ADUs), which is an increase from the nine units completed in 2024. The City issued 15 building permits (14 ADUs and one SB 9 unit). City staff categorized the 15 permitted units as four very low-income, five low-income, three moderate-income, and three above-moderate-income units. These numbers are a decline from the previous four years, which saw over 20 planning permits and at least 16 building permits. 2025 falls short of the city’s goal to build 20 ADUs per year. Bond attributes this to the current state of the market, mortgage rates, and high construction costs. In addition to direct unit construction, Piedmont made significant progress implementing the 77 programs outlined in its Housing Element. Key achievements in 2025 included relaxing zoning restrictions for mixed-use development and adopting the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, adopted in October 2025, provides a framework for the construction of 132 new homes on City-owned land along Moraga Avenue, including road safety improvements, design and landscaping standards, and wildfire safety requirements. The city posted a request for qualifications in May 2026 to begin a search for a development team for Moraga Canyon. The report highlighted the average rent in Piedmont in 2025 was $2,473 per month, the same as reported in 2024. This is still down from the rent prices in 2023 ($2,609) and 2022 ($2,725). Piedmont’s average rent is less than the City of Oakland’s at $2,565 per month for a 769-square-foot unit. California has seen a slight increase in new housing permitted statewide. It’s up 2% from about 119,000 in 2024 to about 121,000 in 2025. There have been gains in affordable multifamily housing and ADU production. Low-income housing saw increases at all stages of development from 2024 to 2025. The number of entitled units increased by 122% from 1,511 to 3,350, permitted units by 7.6% from 3,492 to 3,758, and completed units by 36.4%, from 2,741 to 3,739. The state-mandated targets for the production of new units in Piedmont by the end of 2031 are 587 housing units in the following affordability categories: 238 above moderate income; 92 moderate income; 94 low income; and 163 very low income. Piedmont’s progress will be assessed by the Housing and Community Development department again in June 2027. R e c r e a t i o n 358 Hillside Ave. piedmont.ca.gov/recreation

articles.text: As students return to school, families dropping off and picking up students at the Civic Center may need to adjust their routes due to recent circulation changes. articles.text: Every so often, nature gives us an opportunity to stop what we’re doing, look up, and wonder together. On August 12, a total solar eclipse will be visible from parts of Russia, Greenland, Iceland, and Spain for the first time since 1999. If you happen to be on a European holiday, consider this your reminder to step outside and look up. If not, there’s still plenty you can do to explore the science together from home. A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, temporarily blocking the Sun’s light. Only people sitting directly within a narrow path will experience totality—when the Sun is almost completely hidden, and the sky turns to night—while those outside it will see a partial eclipse or none at all. One of the best places to see the eclipse next week will be in northern Spain, where the maximum eclipse will happen around 8:25 p.m. local time. Because the eclipse there will take place just before sunset, it will appear very low on the horizon—just about one hand’s width above the ground! This rare mix of an eclipsed Sun and the setting sky will produce vibrant sunset colors and a 360-degree twilight glow, making it one of the most visual and unforgettable sky shows of the century! One of the best ways to understand eclipses is through a simple hands-on activity. Using any broad or ring-shaped light that shines from multiple angles at once (your tween’s ring light would work great!), try the Exploratorium’s Science Snack A mother and son safely observe a solar eclipse during an Exploratorium watch party. Eclipses of the Ring Light to recreate the alignments of the Moon, Earth, and Sun. As you reposition the Moon, you’ll discover how eclipses occur, why the path of totality is so narrow, and the different types of shadows the Moon casts. As you play with light and shadow, share what you notice, what you wonder, and try new experiments based on what you want to learn next. What’s happening during an eclipse? Why don’t they happen every month? Why does the Moon sometimes appear to cover the entire Sun and other times only part of it? These kinds of conversations invite us to think like scientists, not by memorizing facts, but by observing, wondering, and building explanations together. Of course, nothing compares to experiencing the eclipse itself. On August 12, the Exploratorium will host a watch party featuring a live broadcast of totality from Spain, alongside scientists and eclipse experts who will help explain what’s happening as it unfolds. Although California won’t experience totality, families can still experience the excitement of this global event while learning the science behind it. Eclipses have a way of bringing people together, and next week is no exception. Let it be a reminder that some of the best learning happens when the world itself becomes the classroom. Sometimes all it takes is looking up, asking questions, and letting curiosity do the rest. articles.text: Once a year, Oaklandish invites adults to relive the magic of Fairyland on their own terms. On Friday, August 14 from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., Fairyland opens its gates for the 14th annual Fairyland for Grownups, an evening of art, entertainment, and pure imagination – an adult-only event. Tickets are on sale now. Fairyland for Grownups transforms the beloved storybook park into an adults-only playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art activations by local visual artists, puppet shows, live DJs, dancing under the stars, and special musical performances by Bay Area heavy-hitting artists. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze, and even ride the beloved Jolly Trolley. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. This year’s lineup includes: DJ SHELLHEART: A Bay Area powerhouse who has spun for the Warriors, Outside Lands, San Francisco Pride, and the Valkyries. DJ SHELLHEART will bring her signature blend of crowd-pleasing hits and immaculate vibes to keep the Merry Meadow dance floor alive all night long. DJ Red Corvette: She is a DJ, music director, and one half of the brilliant minds behind Women Sound Off. With a 10-year journey as a top-tier DJ, she’s rocked at many festivals, nightclubs, and branded events, leaving her mark across Cali and NYC’s hottest spots. Michael Sneed: An East Oakland rapper, producer, and vocalist who uses his vocal superpowers to share narratives about Black joy, personal malaise, reclamation, nostalgia, and the importance of friendships amid the swirling chaos of tech-fueled capitalism. Ovrkast: Oakland-reared rapper, producer, and director Ovrkast is known for his jazz-influenced, sample-heavy sound and fierce independence. After producing for Drake, Earl Sweatshirt, and MAVI, he debuted as a solo artist with Try Again (2020), RESET! (2023), and KAST GOT WINGS (2024) alongside Cardo. His acclaimed 2025 sophomore album, While The Iron Is Hot, cemented his multi-hyphenate status. Beyond music, he directs visuals via his production company, Angr Management, building a creative universe rooted in community and longevity. As part of the annual benefit, guests can purchase the limited-edition Oaklandish Fairyland “Starlit Tee,” featuring a vintage-inspired illustration of Fairyland icons and storybook sets, with delightful characters journeying within its world. The black tee features colorful depictions of “Happy Dragon,” Humpty Dumpty, Willie the Whale, and the famous Fairyland Shoe, accompanied by text that reads “Children’s Fairyland.” The shirt is available to purchase at Oaklandish retail stores and online at oaklandish.com. The event runs for four hours, with bars and activities set up throughout the park. Admission is $30 per person and $25 for Fairyland members. Beer, wine, and cocktails are available for purchase. A selection of Oakland’s finest food vendors will be on hand, offering a variety of delicious bites. Proceeds from Fairyland for Grownups support Children’s Fairyland’s mission to provide affordable access to all children, including outreach programs such as Fairyland for All, summer camp scholarships, and free field trips for underserved communities. While it’s okay to be a kid at heart, a valid 21+ ID is required to attend. Tickets are now available for purchase online at https://fairyland.org/fairyland-for-grownups/. pages.text: Wednesday, August 5, 2026 9 Annual Fairyland for Grownups event on August 14 Once a year, Oaklandish invites adults to relive the magic of Fairyland on their own terms. On Friday, August 14 from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., Fairyland opens its gates for the 14th annual Fairyland for Grownups, an evening of art, entertainment, and pure imagination – an adult-only event. Tickets are on sale now. Fairyland for Grownups transforms the beloved storybook park into an adults-only playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art activations by local visual artists, puppet shows, live DJs, dancing under the stars, and special musical performances by Bay Area heavy-hitting artists. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze, and even ride the beloved Jolly Trolley. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. This year’s lineup includes: DJ SHELLHEART: A Bay Area powerhouse who has spun for the Warriors, Outside Lands, San Francisco Pride, and the Valkyries. DJ SHELLHEART will bring her signature blend of crowd-pleasing hits and immaculate vibes to keep the Merry Meadow dance floor alive all night long. DJ Red Corvette: She is a DJ, music director, and one half of the brilliant minds behind Women Sound Off. With a 10-year journey as a top-tier DJ, she’s rocked at many festivals, nightclubs, and branded events, leaving her mark across Cali and NYC’s hottest spots. Michael Sneed: An East Oakland rapper, producer, and vocalist who uses his vocal superpowers to share narratives about Black joy, personal malaise, reclamation, nostalgia, and the importance of friendships amid the swirling chaos of tech-fueled capitalism. Ovrkast: Oakland-reared rapper, producer, and director Ovrkast is known for his jazz-influenced, sample-heavy sound and fierce independence. After producing for Drake, Earl Sweatshirt, and MAVI, he debuted as a solo artist with Try Again (2020), RESET! (2023), and KAST GOT WINGS (2024) alongside Cardo. His acclaimed 2025 sophomore album, While The Iron Is Hot, cemented his multi-hyphenate status. Beyond music, he directs visuals via his production company, Angr Management, building a creative universe rooted in community and longevity. As part of the annual benefit, guests can purchase the limited-edition Oaklandish Fairyland “Starlit Tee,” featuring a vintage-inspired illustration of Fairyland icons and storybook sets, with delightful characters journeying within its world. The black tee features colorful depictions of “Happy Dragon,” Humpty Dumpty, Willie the Whale, and the famous Fairyland Shoe, accompanied by text that reads “Children’s Fairyland.” The shirt is available to purchase at Oaklandish retail stores and online at oaklandish.com. The event runs for four hours, with bars and activities set up throughout the park. Admission is $30 per person and $25 for Fairyland members. Beer, wine, and cocktails are available for purchase. A selection of Oakland’s finest food vendors will be on hand, offering a variety of delicious bites. Proceeds from Fairyland for Grownups support Children’s Fairyland’s mission to provide affordable access to all children, including outreach programs such as Fairyland for All, summer camp scholarships, and free field trips for underserved communities. While it’s okay to be a kid at heart, a valid 21+ ID is required to attend. Tickets are now available for purchase online at https://fairyland.org/fairyland-for-grownups/. articles.text: Music from some of Studio Ghibli’s best-known animated films will be performed at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, August 9. Sixth Station Trio presents an afternoon concert of chamber arrangements for violin, cello and piano, beginning at 2 p.m. in Samsung Hall. Tickets are included with general museum admission. Based in San Francisco, the Sixth Station Trio consists of violin, cello and piano musicians who have performed together since attending the Ruth Asawa San Francisco School of the Arts. The ensemble made its debut at Grace Cathedral in 2023 with a sold-out program featuring music from Studio Ghibli films. Founded in 1985, Studio Ghibli is one of Japan’s most influential animation studios, known for films that combine hand-drawn animation, imaginative storytelling and memorable musical scores. The program features music composed primarily by Joe Hisaishi, the longtime collaborator of filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki. The concert will include selections from films such as Howl’s Moving Castle, Spirited Away, Kiki’s Delivery Service, My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, Ponyo, Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, Laputa: Castle in the Sky, Arrietty and The Boy and the Heron. Audience members can expect to hear pieces including “Merry-Go-Round of Life,” “One Summer’s Day” and “A Town with an Ocean View,” as well as familiar Nintendo theme songs. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/sixth-station-trio-august-9/. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) newest exhibition Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs explores the evolving dialogue between movement and photography. Feel the Beat, on view now through January 31, 2027, highlights photography’s role in shaping how dance is recorded and remembered, and how dancers have inspired photographers to view movement in a different medium. The new exhibition includes items from SFMOMA’s permanent collection, opening with a gallery devoted to Irving Penn’s images of Anna Halprin and the San Francisco Dancers’ Workshop, as well as pictures that reflect Halprin’s experimental approach to dance. The second gallery turns to Kamaitachi, the partnership between Japanese photographer Eikoh Hosoe and Butoh founder Tatsumi Hijikata. The final section of the exhibition explores “nightlife,” with Malick Sidibé’s photographs of dancing at parties in Mali, as well as photos by Nan Goldin, Larry Fink, Janine Gordon, Weegee, Imogen Cunningham, Barbara Morgan, Robert Rauschenberg, Richard Avedon and more. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibitions/. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art Museum patron views Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs exhibit at SFMOMA.

The Treasure Island Museum will host a swing dance fundraiser on Saturday, September 26, to support the museum’s educational programs and historical exhibitions. Held from 7 to 10 p.m. at the museum, 39 Treasure Island Road in San Francisco, the evening will celebrate the glamour of the Swing Era and the golden age of air travel. The event is organized by the Treasure Island Museum Board. Live entertainment will be provided by the Nick Rossi Swing Six, a jazz and salsa ensemble specializing in music from the 1930s and 1940s. Guests will also enjoy classic cocktails from Gold Bar Distillery and a onenight-only exhibition featuring rarely displayed artifacts from the museum’s Pan American Airways collection. The museum, housed in a historic building dating to the height of the Swing Era, will serve as the backdrop for the evening’s festivities. Attendees are encouraged to wear festive or vintage-inspired attire, although period dress is not required. Prizes will be awarded for the most authentic and creative vintage outfits. Proceeds from the fundraiser will benefit the museum’s educational programming and ongoing efforts to preserve and interpret the history of Treasure Island through exhibits and public outreach. The fundraiser will take place Saturday, September 26, from 7 to 10 p.m. at the Treasure Island Museum, 39 Treasure Island Road, San Francisco. Tickets are available at https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/our-swing-dance-benefit-inhistoric-building-one.

articles.text: Margaret Cho Comedian and actor Margaret Cho will perform her new stand-up show “Choligarchy” at Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Roda Theatre for a limited six-performance run September 15 through 19. The engagement marks Cho’s return to the East Bay with a new hour of political and personal comedy. Performances begin Tuesday, September 15, and continue through Saturday, September 19. Tickets went on sale to the general public July 31, following early access for Berkeley Rep subscribers. Cho describes “Choligarchy” as a return to her roots as a political comedian, drawing on current events and social issues. The show explores topics including politics, racism, sexism, homophobia and activism through Cho’s blend of sharp social commentary and personal storytelling. “I’m so frustrated with the state of the union, and I know the only weapon I have is humor,” Cho said in a press release. “We are being taken over by the richest people in the world, but the one thing they cannot afford is jokes at their expense. I want to fight fascism with everything I have. This will be my most blistering and brutally honest show yet.” A San Francisco native, Cho first gained national attention in the 1990s through her stand-up comedy and the television sitcom All-American Girl, the first U.S. network sitcom centered on an Asian American family. Over a career spanning more than three decades, she has earned five Grammy and Emmy nominations and built a reputation for tackling subjects such as identity, addiction, family and LGBTQ+ rights in her performances. In addition to stand-up, Cho has appeared in numerous television series and films, including Fire Island, The Flight Attendant, Hacks and Will Trent. Her recent film All That We Love premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival, and she is also set to appear in the second season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians. The Roda Theatre performances are scheduled for September 15 through September 19 at Berkeley Repertory Theatre. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: The Grammy Award-winning gospel group Take 6 will return to San Francisco for a four-concert engagement at SFJAZZ’s Miner Auditorium from August 13 through 16. The Alabama-based sextet is known for its intricate a cappella harmonies, blending gospel, jazz, R&B, pop and blues. The performances celebrate more than 45 years of the group’s career, which has earned 10 Grammy Awards and established Take 6 as one of the most influential vocal ensembles in contemporary gospel music. Founded in 1980 at Oakwood College in Huntsville, Alabama, by tenor Claude McKnight, the group began by performing at churches before signing with Atlantic Records. Their self-titled 1988 debut album won three Grammy Awards and earned a nomination for Best New Artist. Over the decades, Take 6 has released 15 albums and collaborated with artists including Ray Charles, Ella Fitzgerald, Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder and Jacob Collier. The ensemble has also contributed music to the soundtracks of films including Do the Right Thing and Boyz n the Hood, while performing for audiences around the world and multiple U.S. presidents. The group’s most recent album, Iconic, released on its independent Sono label, reached No. 1 on the Billboard Jazz Albums chart. The SFJAZZ concerts will feature founding members Claude McKnight and Mark Kibble alongside the current lineup, performing selections that showcase the group’s signature vocal arrangements and gospel-inspired repertoire. articles.text: The Flower Piano festival will return to the San Francisco Botanical Garden September 10 through 20, bringing live performances and public piano installations to the 55-acre garden. The annual event features 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the garden, where visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform or play the instruments during designated open play sessions. Flower Piano was created in 2015 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Ffortissimo and Dean Mermell in collaboration with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The festival has since become an annual event at the botanical garden. This year’s lineup includes daily performances by La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9, the San Francisco Ballet School and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, whose repertoire blends hip-hop, jazz and classical music. The 2026 festival also includes an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, featuring seating, food and beverages, and evening performances. During open play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels to use. Attendees are encouraged to bring picnic blankets as seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and tickets, is available at https://gggp.org/flowerpiano. The beloved festival returns to Golden Gate Park next month.

articles.text: The Sheep Detectives is the best movie about intelligent sheep since Shaun the Sheep! With actors like Bryan Cranston, Hugh Jackman, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, director Kyle Balda had his work cut out for him, balancing a big cast while still making sure every character got their moment. Hugh Jackman’s character, George Hardy, lives a simple life as a shepherd for a flock of sheep to whom he gave individual names, treating them less like animals and more like a family he talks to every night. Despite his merits, he is not immune to smalltown drama, and it becomes clear early on that his quiet life is not as peaceful as it looks from the outside. All of the actors brought this world together; the proper voice actor for each sheep brings personality to the fuzzy fourlegged characters in the film. The soft and confident voice of Louis-Dreyfus gave her character, Lily, the proper attitude of a sheep prone to lead, but with much to learn. It was easy to root for Lily even when she was in the wrong. The great work of the casting directors, Lucy Bevan and Emily Brockmann, is Hugh Jackman as George Hardy in the Sheep Detectives heard and seen in every character, down to the smaller roles in the flock who still manage to feel like real personalities instead of background noise. One of the few problems is the pacing at the beginning and the ending. George dies at a strange time, about a quarter of the way through the movie, and the rest of the film feels rushed, as if it’s hurrying to fit the investigation and the ending into the time it has left. It’s not that the mystery itself suffers, but you can feel the arrow of time speeding up in a way that doesn’t quite match the careful setup at the beginning. The mystery stayed a mystery through the entire movie, which is exactly what a film like this needs to do to keep you guessing. All of the suspects had good motives and opportunities to kill George, so there was never a moment where the answer felt obvious. For a kids’ murder-mystery, the movie never loses its message: showing and telling those you love makes them better people. If you are into children’s mysteries and do not need to feel like the smartest detective in the room, this movie is for you. The Sheep Detectives . Directed by Kyle Balda. articles.text: For more than four decades, North Berkeley Imports has quietly shaped the way Americans think about fine wine. Founded in 1979 and based in Berkeley, California, the importer has earned a national reputation for seeking out family-owned estates that faithfully express the character of their vineyards rather than chasing international trends. Its portfolio reflects a philosophy that great wines are made in the vineyard, with an emphasis on sustainable farming, traditional winemaking, and producers who are deeply connected to their land. Few importers have done more to introduce American consumers to the classic wines of France’s Loire Valley. North Berkeley Imports represents many of the region’s most respected growers, helping wine lovers discover everything from the mineral-driven Sauvignon Blancs of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé to the age-worthy Chenin Blancs of Vouvray, Savennières, and Anjou. The company’s selections consistently emphasize authenticity, balance, and value, proving that some of the world’s most distinctive wines need not be the most expensive. For retailers, sommeliers, and adventurous consumers alike, the North Berkeley Imports name has become a trusted guide to producers whose wines capture the unique terroir of the Loire and many of Europe’s other great wine regions. For many wine lovers, France’s Loire Valley is synonymous with elegant white wines that emphasize freshness, balance, and a remarkable sense of place. Stretching more than 600 miles along the Loire River from central France to the Atlantic Ocean, the region produces an extraordinary range of whites that are among the world’s finest values. Perhaps the best known is Sauvignon Blanc from the neighboring appellations of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. These wines are celebrated for their vibrant citrus flavors, crisp acidity, and distinctive mineral character that reflects the region’s limestone and flint soils. They are natural companions to oysters, goat cheese, and fresh seafood. Farther west, Chenin Blanc reigns supreme. Few grapes are as versatile. In appellations such as Vouvray and Montlouis-sur-Loire, Chenin Blanc can produce bone-dry wines with notes of green apple, quince, honey, and chamomile, as well as sparkling wines and luscious dessert bottlings capable of aging for decades. In Anjou and Saumur, the grape takes on yet another personality, offering rich texture balanced by lively acidity. Near the Atlantic coast, the Melon de Bourgogne grape gives rise to Muscadet, a light-bodied white that is often aged “sur lie,” resting on its yeast lees to develop extra texture and a subtle bready complexity. It remains one of the classic partners for shellfish and is a favorite in the seafood restaurants of western France. What unites the Loire’s white wines is their emphasis on elegance rather than power. They are 1505 Shattuck Ave., Berkeley, CA retail@northberkeleyimports.com The Loire Valley is home to Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc and Muscadet.

articles.text: Last Wednesday, 49 walkers and two K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra for a Piedmont Recreation Department Walking on Wednesdays outing featuring music, local history and a little climbing. As part of an effort to ensure the activity’s long-term future, more walkers are taking turns leading the group. Max Becker led this week’s walk. The group also thanked Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kellogg and Matt Gerhardt for leading walks in July. Mary Carter, Gerhardt, Jack Fischrup and Sean Brient will lead the four August walks, and Lori Austin has been helping write walk summaries. Becker grew up in Piedmont and attended Piedmont schools. After he and his wife returned from Washington, D.C., he joined Walking on Wednesdays to reconnect with the community. He also brought a musical background to the morning. For the past 15 years, Becker has performed internationally with the rock band SWMRS, which includes his younger brothers, Cole and Cade Becker. The band began while they were students at Piedmont High School. Rather than leading a walk focused on real estate, Becker planned a musical route through town and the high school campus. Sitara explored her new habitat for the first time on July 29. Oakland Zoo’s rescue program extends far beyond any single case, and for over 30 years the Zoo has played a unique role among accredited institutions. The Zoo regularly supports law enforcement and animal welfare agencies through case consultation, emergency response, placement coordination, and, when possible, by providing a forever home. When the Zoo is unable to provide a home, it stabilizes rescued animals and coordinates with a network of accredited facilities to ensure appropriate lifelong care. Over the past few weeks, the Zoo has worked with partners, including Performing Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) in California and Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge in Arkansas, to place three of the tigers and determine the best possible outcome for all those transferred. Both sanctuaries are accredited by the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries (GFAS) and are members of the Big Cat Sanctuary Alliance. Each of the five tiger’s outcome reflects individualized holistic care decisions based on their health, behavior, and longterm welfare: A 14-year-old female white tiger, suffering from significant visual impairment due to inbreeding, received intermediate care at Oakland Zoo. Once she was physically prepared, she relocated to Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge. White tigers result from a rare genetic mutation called leucism. Breeding these tigers involves pairing two individuals with recessive genes to produce white-coated offspring. However, in these breeding programs, the animals are commonly related, leading to inbreeding that can cause myriad health issues, including blindness. A male, white-and-Bengal tiger mix, estimated to be 11 years old, and a male Siberian tiger mix, estimated to be 13 years old, were relocated to PAWS, which specializes in providing expert, lifelong care for older and physically challenged animals with complex needs. A female generic tiger, estimated to have been 16 years old, came to Oakland Zoo experiencing end-stage arthritis and spinal disease, causing extreme lameness and neurologic deficits in her hind limbs. She received intensive care at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, but her condition did not respond to treatment despite continuous effort from the veterinary and animal care teams; ultimately, the kindest option for this tiger was humane euthanasia. The new resident, Sitara, has begun working with her Animal Care staff to train and develop the skills she needs to explore her new habitat. She is learning to navigate pools, a waterfall, raised platforms, grass, and vegetation - all things she hasn’t had before. The Zoo will continue to post updates on social media about her journey. Additionally, the Zoo is initiating a program to help her build trust and resilience in response to negative experiences with past caretakers, while monitoring her behavioral and mental health challenges. “Projects like this remind us that animal welfare is profoundly personal, and one of the most meaningful things we can do is change the life of one individual. These tigers have been given a future with greater stability, greater opportunity, and greater peace,” said Amy Phelps, Zoological Manager at Oakland Zoo. The Zoo has cared for numerous big cats, including tigers, for decades, providing a safe refuge and raising awareness among visitors, members, and the commuSitara lies in the grass of her habitat at the Oakland Zoo. nity about the challenges posed by private ownership and trafficked wildlife in human care. The arrival of these rescued tigers continues the legacy of more than a dozen Oakland Zoo big cat rescues and provides an opportunity to share new stories that inspire compassion and support higher standards and regulations for big cats and other captive wildlife nationwide. This latest effort follows over 30 years of the Zoo’s dedication to protecting wildlife and to closing facilities involved in the mistreatment, malnutrition, and inadequate care of exotic animals. Oakland Zoo has played a crucial role in rescuing and caring for a wide range of animals, including reptiles, amphibians, mammals, and birds. Since 2021, the Oakland Zoo has received more than 250 requests from wildlife agencies, advocacy groups, and animal rescue organizations for assistance with rescue operations. These efforts aim to support victims of the wildlife pet trade, roadside zoos, and other forms of trafficking. The Zoo’s commitment to rescues requires significant financial and staff investment, especially due to the unpredictable nature of the health and wellbeing of the individuals rescued. The zoo estimates that in 2025 they spent more than $100,000 on rescue work, work that is only possible through philanthropy. Progress has been made since the passage of the Big Cat Public Safety Act, signed into law in 2022, which has significantly contributed to animal protection efforts. The act has curbed private ownership and commercial breeding of big cats in the U.S. It has decreased “cub petting” operations and prevented new private owners from acquiring these animals, helping to reduce illegal activity and protect exotic wildlife. Sitara and the other recently transferred tigers serve as reminders that more can be done to protect big cats and to educate visitors and supporters about responsible choices. The core issue in the tiger crisis is the breeding of big cats to supply the cub-petting industry, including pay-to-pose photo opportunities. articles.text: July 15, 1969 to July 25, 2026 Ronald Scott Mosbaugh passed away on July 25, 2026, after several years struggling through congestive heart and kidney failure. Known to everyone as Scott, he was born in Castro Valley’s Eden Hospital on July 15, 1969 to Nancy Heishman Mosbaugh of Castro Valley and Ronald Mosbaugh of Joplin, Missouri. A lifelong resident of the East Bay, he was raised in a multigenerational home in Castro Valley with his maternal grandmother and grandfather Helen and Harvey Heishman, his great-grandmother Lily Schatt and mother Nancy. He graduated from Castro Valley High in 1987, and attended Chabot College before getting his degree in history from Cal State Hayward. After graduation he contributed to multiple tech start up companies including art.com and Cytiva Software. In 2008 his life pivoted, as he bought his first home in Oakland, changed careers and married his girlfriend of three years, Elizabeth (Liz) Tuuri. Leaving the tech startups behind, he settled into the California Public Utilities Commission in San Francisco where he served under the last eleven commissioners, most recently Matt Baker, working until the day he died. Liz and Scott’s only child, Chris, was born three years later. The family moved to Piedmont in 2016 as Chris entered school. A lover of history, bad puns, Disney, Pixar, video and RPG board games, his favorite place in the world was Disneyland. His fondest memory was a three hour Ronald Scott Mosbaugh Friendsgiving dinner where he and a friend spent the entire meal speaking in nothing but puns. He enjoyed his time with his family (preferably at a Disney park) and was deadicated to paranormal investigating, always looking for signs of life beyond death. We hope he has found it peacefully now, somewhere as wonderful as the Magic Kingdom itself. He is survived by his mother Nancy, his father Ron, sisters Carrie and Sunny, brother Jeff, sisterin-law Kim, nephews Johnny and Conal, niece Shaelyn, sister-in-law Laura Tuuri, and his wife Liz Tuuri-Mosbaugh and son Chris. A memorial service will be held on the evening of August 24 from 4 to 7 p.m. at the Lake Temescal Boathouse. His family is grateful for the kindness and support shown during this time.

articles.text: Finn Zijlstra, Zara Hinson, Josh Estrada, and Theodore Mehlinger Eisemon Happy people, a crew working together, operating a boat, docking and casting off, navigating, steering, cooking and washing dishes together, and bursting into song like in an old-fashioned Broadway musical. I was part of that joy as a guest for five of the 14 days of the annual Summer Cruise aboard the Sea Scout boat Seafox. Sea Scouts is part of Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) for all genders, ages 14 through 20. The scouts planned the cruise and sailed the 67-foot powerboat under the watchful eyes of US Coast Guard Licensed Skipper Ken Shupe, who started in scouting as a young boy and has been Skipper since 2014, growing the program from a few active scouts to more than two dozen. Skipper Shupe said that they average almost 90 days of water activities per year, from an inflatable Zodiac to rowing and sailing dinghies, 26-foot rowing whaleboats, a ski boat, a 41-foot sailboat, and a 67-foot powerboat. He said, “We are here to give scouts confidence to be leaders to their peers, communities, and future careers…” He emphasized that the scouts have “Fun and learn something along the way.” Sea Scout Ship 9 Committee Chair Will Pallas emphasized Sea Scouts’ coed youth leadership and maritime and life skills. articles.text: Nature Play Area hand-drawn illustration by artist Ana Gadish-Linares Following the removal of the unsafe swings in 2024, Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Fall Fundraising Campaign successfully focused on securing funds for the swing replacement. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings. This project will transform an underused section of the park into a vibrant outdoor learning environment featuring climbing logs, native plants, and hands-on natural play elements for children to explore. PBF has worked since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces that foster a strong sense of pride and community. In addition to its many valuable contributions to parks, tot lots, schools, and recreational facilities, PBF also brings the community together to celebrate the Piedmont Lights Up ceremony every December. PBF looks forward to sharing more updates as they work to improve the community’s outdoor spaces. To learn more about PBF’s efforts to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park, visit their website: https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/ways-to-give/.
